title: Russia’s gray shadow over the Black Sea
text:
Russia’s gray shadow over the Black Sea
Deadly drone attacks on merchant ships off the coast of two NATO countries hint that the Kremlin has opened a new front on Europe’s zone of security. European leaders are rushing to provide better defenses in a key global passageway for grain exports.
The European Union’s long project to build the continent into a fortified zone of peace and prosperity has hit a new pitfall. Over the past two weeks, the war in Ukraine has expanded far into the Black Sea. Several merchant ships carrying grain and other civilian cargo were struck by drones – widely viewed as Russian – off the shores of two NATO members, Bulgaria and Romania. Nearly two dozen sailors from many countries were either killed or are missing.
“The Kremlin is testing the EU and Nato, and will act depending on the results of the testing,” a popular Ukrainian blogger, Boryslav Bereza, wrote on Facebook.
The attacks hint at Russia expanding its reach across Europe, one that relies on hybrid or gray-zone warfare tactics such as disinformation campaigns, drone strikes, cyberattacks, and sabotage— that fall short of open war, much like the ongoing “shadow war” in the Baltic states and Arctic.
With both Bulgaria and Romania now alarmed, European leaders have rushed to respond. NATO is weighing whether to move anti-drone defenses to the Black Sea, which serves as a gateway between Europe, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean. Bulgaria, whose prime minister is often seen as pro-Russia, now wants those defenses and has confronted the Kremlin’s ambassador to Sofia about the ship attacks.
“Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea,” NATO’s secretary-general, Mark Rutte, said Thursday, “adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Last year, the EU kicked off a plan to prevent the Black Sea from becoming a Russian stronghold that includes protection for data cables and civilian ships. Turkey, which has control over the Bosporus, has formed closer ties with Romania and Bulgaria to boost safety in the region.
Europe’s big task now is helping commercial vessels operate in the Black Sea without sparking a major clash with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Before the war in Ukraine started 4 1/2 years ago, some 20% of the world’s wheat exports and 15% of maize exports passed through the Black Sea.
Keeping these essential supplies flowing is key not only to the world, but for Europe’s plan to ensure a zone of peace and prosperity.
